theme: The LORD is my shepherd, rest and restoration
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 23. It is probably the most familiar psalm in the Bible, so read it as if for the first time. Slow down at each line. Notice the change from third person (“he”) to second person (“you”) in the middle of verse 4, as the psalm moves from talking about the shepherd to talking to him.
settingTheScene: Psalm 23 comes at the beginning of this week as a reflection on the rest God gives. Israel is settling into the land, and the shepherd imagery of this psalm captures what the land of promise is meant to be: a place of green pastures and still waters under the care of a good shepherd. David, who wrote this psalm, was himself a shepherd boy before he was a king, so he knew what a shepherd’s work involved. He uses it to describe the LORD’s care. This psalm is often read at funerals, but it is a psalm for the living as much as for the dying. It is about what it means to lack nothing because of who God is.
observation: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (v. 1).
He makes me lie down in green pastures and leads me beside still waters (v. 2).
“He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake” (v. 3).
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (v. 4).
The shepherd’s “rod and staff” comfort me (v. 4).
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows” (v. 5).
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life” (v. 6).
“I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever” (v. 6).
interpretation:
The opening line carries the whole psalm. “The LORD is my shepherd.” Everything that follows is an unpacking of what it means. “I shall not want” does not mean “I will get everything I desire.” It means “I will lack nothing I truly need, because I belong to him.” A shepherd takes responsibility for his sheep. He finds food, water, rest, and safety. Sheep can do none of this for themselves. They are among the most dependent animals, and David says that is a good thing, because the one who looks after us is the LORD.

Verses 2-3 describe the shepherd’s gentle care: green pastures, still waters, a restored soul. These are images of rest, a theme that fits the week well. The shepherd leads. The sheep follow. Note that the paths are “paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.” The shepherd guides his flock in the right way, and his reputation is tied to it. He will not lose those he has promised to keep.

Then comes the valley. David does not claim that the good shepherd leads only through pleasant places. There is a valley of deep darkness, and it is on the path. But look at what changes there. The language shifts in the middle of verse 4 from “he” to “you.” In the dark, David stops talking about God and starts talking to him. “You are with me.” That is the heart of the psalm. The comfort is not an absence of danger but the presence of the shepherd. His rod defends against predators, and his staff guides and rescues. The same tools that protect also comfort.

Verse 5 changes the metaphor from a shepherd to a host. The table is set “in the presence of my enemies.” God’s hospitality is not hidden from those who oppose us. He anoints and fills. The cup overflows. This is the language of extravagant welcome.

The last verse promises that goodness and mercy will pursue David, not just follow. The Hebrew verb is “chase.” All his days, God’s kindness is on his heels. And the final destination is the house of the LORD forever.

For Christians, the shepherd has a name. Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). The psalm takes on its fullest meaning in him. He walked through the valley of death himself, so that when we pass through it, we find him already there.
connection: The shepherd image is used of God in Genesis 48:15 and 49:24, and of Israel’s leaders in Ezekiel 34, where God promises to shepherd his people himself. Jesus claims the title in John 10:1-18, and Hebrews 13:20 calls him “the great shepherd of the sheep.” The table before enemies recalls the covenant meals of Exodus 24 and anticipates the Lord’s Supper. Revelation 7:17 says the Lamb “will be their shepherd.”
application:
Read this psalm aloud once today, slowly. Then tell the Lord one area of your life where you have been behaving like a sheep who thinks it must provide for itself. Hand it over.

If you are in a valley right now, notice the pronoun change. Try praying the second half of verse 4 in your own words: “You are with me.” Say it out loud.

If you are in a season of green pastures, receive them with thanks. Don’t rush past rest. Ask the Lord what he might be restoring in you.

Finally, ask who you could shepherd this week. A friend, a child, or a younger believer may need your presence. We carry the shepherd’s care to others.
prayerPrompts: Tell the Lord what you lack, and what you need him to shepherd.
Ask him to restore your soul, and to remind you he is with you in the dark valley.
